lesson.title: Finding the Right Pair of Numbers: Factoring Trinomials
lesson.summary: Factoring a trinomial x^2 + bx + c means finding two numbers that multiply to c and add to b, then writing the trinomial as two binomials built from that pair.
lesson.body:
A trinomial in the form x^2 + bx + c, where the leading coefficient is 1, can often be factored into two binomials by reversing the FOIL process. The introduction to factoring earlier in this unit previewed this exact idea with x^2 + 5x + 6; now the method gets a closer, more general look. The approach is to find two numbers, call them p and q, that multiply together to give c and add together to give b. Once found, the trinomial factors as (x + p)(x + q).

This method works because it is simply FOIL run backward. Expanding (x + p)(x + q) with FOIL gives x^2 + qx + px + pq, and combining the middle terms gives x^2 + (p + q)x + pq. Matching this to x^2 + bx + c shows that p + q must equal b and pq must equal c, which is exactly the condition used to search for p and q in the first place.

Apply this to x^2 - x - 12. Here b is negative 1 and c is negative 12, so the two numbers must multiply to negative 12 and add to negative 1. Testing pairs of factors of 12, negative 4 and 3 work: negative 4 times 3 is negative 12, and negative 4 plus 3 is negative 1. So the trinomial factors as (x - 4)(x + 3).

Check by expanding (x - 4)(x + 3) with FOIL: First is x times x, giving x^2. Outer is x times 3, giving 3x. Inner is negative 4 times x, giving negative 4x. Last is negative 4 times 3, giving negative 12. Adding these, x^2 + 3x - 4x - 12, the middle terms combine to negative x, giving back x^2 - x - 12, which matches the original trinomial exactly. A second example shows the all positive case: for x^2 + 7x + 10, the numbers must multiply to 10 and add to 7, and 5 and 2 satisfy both, since 5 times 2 is 10 and 5 plus 2 is 7, giving (x + 5)(x + 2). Expanding confirms it: x^2 + 2x + 5x + 10 combines to x^2 + 7x + 10.

The signs of b and c tell you what kind of pair to look for before you even start testing numbers. If c is positive and b is positive, both numbers are positive. If c is positive and b is negative, both numbers are negative. If c is negative, as in the first example above, the two numbers have opposite signs, and the sign of the larger one matches the sign of b. This same number pair strategy is the backbone for two special cases covered separately later in this unit, difference of squares and perfect square trinomials, where the numbers follow an especially predictable pattern. When the leading coefficient of a trinomial is not 1, the search for matching numbers becomes more involved and is typically handled with a more advanced technique beyond this section.

Not every trinomial has a matching pair of integers at all. For x^2 + x + 1, you would need two numbers that multiply to 1 and add to 1; the only integer pair with a product of 1 is 1 and 1, or negative 1 and negative 1, and neither pair adds to 1. When no such pair exists, the trinomial simply does not factor over the integers, and it is sometimes called prime for that reason. Recognizing when to stop searching is as important as knowing how to search in the first place.
